description: Process and decision modelling (BPMN 2.0, DMN, CMMN) plus business architecture views (capabilities, value streams, information, people). For architects who model processes or connect strategy to change.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::01 BPMN Core Elements
notes.front: What is BPMN and what does it standardise?
notes.back: Business Process Model and Notation: an OMG standard notation whose diagrams mean the same regardless of modelling tool.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::01 BPMN Core Elements
notes.front: What are the three core flow-object categories in BPMN?
notes.back:
Events (circle) — something happens
Activities (rounded rectangle) — work is done
Gateways (diamond) — flow branches/merges

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::01 BPMN Core Elements
notes.front: BPMN: sequence flow vs message flow?
notes.back: Sequence flow (solid arrow): order of steps within one pool. Message flow (dashed, open arrowhead): communication between pools — never inside one.
notes.analogy: Sequence flow is passing a folder to a colleague's desk; message flow is posting a letter to another company.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::01 BPMN Core Elements
notes.front: What do pools and lanes represent in BPMN?
notes.back: Pool: a participant (organisation, system). Lane: a sub-partition of a pool showing which role/department/system does each step.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::01 BPMN Core Elements
notes.front: What is a black-box pool and when do you use one?
notes.back: A pool with no internal detail, for a participant whose internal steps are irrelevant or unknown — only its message flows matter.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::01 BPMN Core Elements
notes.front: What are BPMN artifacts?
notes.back: Elements that add information without affecting flow: annotations (text notes) and groups (dashed box, no formal semantics).

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::01 BPMN Core Elements
notes.front: BPMN: data object vs data store?
notes.back: Data object: information flowing through one process instance (e.g. a document). Data store: persistent repository (e.g. a database) that outlives instances.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: How are BPMN start, intermediate and end events drawn?
notes.back:
Start: thin single circle
Intermediate: double circle
End: thick single circle

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: BPMN: catching vs throwing event?
notes.back: Catching (unfilled icon) waits for a trigger, e.g. a message arriving. Throwing (filled icon) fires one, e.g. sending a message.
notes.extra: Start events catch; end events throw; intermediates can be either.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: BPMN: error vs escalation event?
notes.back: Error: a critical failure — a caught error interrupts the activity. Escalation: a non-critical heads-up to a higher level — can be non-interrupting.
notes.analogy: Error = the machine broke, stop the line. Escalation = tell the manager we're running late, keep working.
notes.extra: Other triggers: message, timer, signal, conditional, compensation, link, terminate, multiple.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: What does a BPMN compensation event do?
notes.back: Triggers the undo (compensation) activities of steps that already completed — e.g. refund a payment when a booking is cancelled.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: What are message start and end events used for?
notes.back: Message start: begins an instance when a message arrives (e.g. order received). Message end: sends a message as the instance ends (e.g. confirmation).

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: BPMN: error end event vs terminate end event?
notes.back: Error end: ends the path and throws a named error to be caught elsewhere. Terminate end: immediately kills the whole instance, all parallel paths, no error.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: What is a BPMN boundary event?
notes.back: An event attached to an activity's edge that catches a trigger while that activity is running.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: Boundary events: interrupting vs non-interrupting?
notes.back: Interrupting (solid double circle): cancels the activity. Non-interrupting (dashed double circle): activity continues while a parallel path starts.
notes.analogy: Interrupting: the fire alarm ends the meeting. Non-interrupting: a reminder ping you deal with while the meeting goes on.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: A review task must keep running, but a reminder should go out after 2 days. Which event do you attach?
notes.back: A non-interrupting timer boundary event: the reminder path starts in parallel and the review continues. An interrupting one would cancel the review.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: What can a BPMN timer event be configured with?
notes.back: A specific date/time, a duration (wait 3 days) or a recurring cycle.
notes.extra: As start: scheduled trigger. Intermediate: delay. Boundary: deadline.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: BPMN: signal vs message event?
notes.back: Signal: broadcast, no specific target — every listener catches it. Message: addressed from one sender to one receiver.
notes.analogy: Signal = a radio broadcast; message = a registered letter.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: A system shutdown must cancel every pending order instance at once. Message or signal event, and why?
notes.back: A signal: it is broadcast to all listening instances. A message targets exactly one receiver, so you would need one per order.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::02 BPMN Events
notes.front: What is a BPMN link event for?
notes.back: A throw/catch pair acting as an on-page connector, continuing a sequence flow elsewhere without long crossing arrows.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::03 BPMN Gateways
notes.front: What does an exclusive (XOR) gateway do?
notes.back: Routes to exactly one outgoing path based on conditions (or a default). Diamond, empty or with 'X'.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::03 BPMN Gateways
notes.front: What does a parallel (AND) gateway do?
notes.back: Split: activates all paths, no conditions. Join: waits for all incoming paths. Diamond with '+'.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::03 BPMN Gateways
notes.front: What does an inclusive (OR) gateway do?
notes.back: Split: activates one or more paths whose conditions are true. Join: waits for all paths that were actually activated. Diamond with 'O'.
notes.extra: Pitfall: the trickiest gateway to model and implement correctly.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::03 BPMN Gateways
notes.front: What goes wrong if an exclusive merge follows a parallel split?
notes.back: The merge passes on each arriving path separately, so everything after it runs once per branch instead of once.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::03 BPMN Gateways
notes.front: What goes wrong if a parallel join follows an exclusive split?
notes.back: The join waits for all incoming paths, but the split only activates one, so the process deadlocks. Match the join type to the split type.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::03 BPMN Gateways
notes.front: Event-based gateway vs exclusive gateway?
notes.back: Both pick one path, but event-based decides by which event happens first (message vs timer), not by data conditions.
notes.analogy: Waiting at the door for either the courier or a 30-minute timeout — whichever comes first decides what you do next.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::03 BPMN Gateways
notes.front: An order waits for a customer reply or 7 days, whichever comes first. Which gateway and elements model this?
notes.back: An event-based gateway followed by a message catch event and a timer catch event; the first to occur wins and the other is discarded.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::03 BPMN Gateways
notes.front: When is a complex gateway used?
notes.back: For routing rules the standard gateways can't express, e.g. 'continue when 3 of 5 paths arrive'; the rule is described in text.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::04 BPMN Activities & Sub-processes
notes.text:
BPMN task types:
{{c1::User task}}: a human, via an application UI
{{c2::Manual task}}: a human, without system support
{{c3::Service task}}: automatic system/service call
{{c4::Script task}}: script run by the process engine
{{c5::Business rule task}}: invokes a decision (often DMN)
{{c6::Send / Receive task}}: sends or waits for a message

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::04 BPMN Activities & Sub-processes
notes.front: Embedded sub-process vs call activity?
notes.back: Embedded: drawn inline, exists only in its parent. Call activity: invokes a separate, reusable, independently versioned process.
notes.analogy: Inline code vs calling a library function.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::04 BPMN Activities & Sub-processes
notes.front: What is an event sub-process?
notes.back: A sub-process inside a parent but not connected by sequence flow; it starts when its own start trigger fires while the parent runs, optionally interrupting it.
notes.analogy: Like an office fire drill procedure: not part of the normal workflow, but it can start at any moment during the day.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::04 BPMN Activities & Sub-processes
notes.front: What is a transaction sub-process?
notes.back: All-or-nothing: on normal completion it commits; on cancel it triggers compensation of the completed steps.
notes.analogy: Like a database transaction rollback, but done by business undo steps (refund, cancel) rather than the DB.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::04 BPMN Activities & Sub-processes
notes.front: What does the multi-instance marker on an activity mean?
notes.back: The activity runs once per item in a collection — parallel (three vertical bars) or sequential (three horizontal bars).

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::04 BPMN Activities & Sub-processes
notes.front: What is an ad-hoc sub-process?
notes.back: Activities without fixed sequence flow, run in any order until a completion condition — for unstructured work.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::05 Modeling Method
notes.front: Real-Life BPMN: who are 'the customers of a process model', and why does it matter?
notes.back: The people who read and use the diagram (business, developers, auditors). Design each diagram for its audience, not for maximal completeness.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::05 Modeling Method
notes.front: What is a BPMN monolith and how do you fix it?
notes.back: One oversized diagram for a whole end-to-end process. Split models along domain boundaries, connected via call activities or message flow.
notes.analogy: Like a single 5,000-line function: technically complete, practically unreadable — split it into modules.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::05 Modeling Method
notes.front: Descriptive vs executable BPMN models?
notes.back: Descriptive: for human understanding, never run. Executable: precise enough to deploy on a process engine (e.g. Camunda).

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::05 Modeling Method
notes.front: Why can a descriptive model not simply be deployed on a process engine?
notes.back: It is written for human understanding and omits executable detail such as precise conditions, data mappings and task implementations. It must be made technically precise first.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::05 Modeling Method
notes.front: BPMN: orchestration, collaboration, choreography diagrams?
notes.back: Orchestration: one participant's process. Collaboration: several pools linked by message flow. Choreography: only the message exchanges, no internal steps.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::06 DMN & CMMN
notes.front: What is DMN and what problem does it solve?
notes.back: Decision Model and Notation (OMG): models decision logic separately, so rules don't get buried in gateway conditions.
notes.analogy: The process is the assembly line; DMN is the tax table it consults — change the table without rebuilding the line.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::06 DMN & CMMN
notes.front: What are the two main DMN diagram types?
notes.back:
Decision Requirements Diagram (DRD): decisions and their dependencies.
Decision table: the rule rows for one decision.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::06 DMN & CMMN
notes.front: What is a DMN hit policy?
notes.back: How multiple matching rows are resolved, e.g. Unique, First, Collect, Priority.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::06 DMN & CMMN
notes.front: How does a BPMN process call a DMN decision?
notes.back: A business rule task references the decision; the engine passes inputs, evaluates the table and returns the result to the process.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::06 DMN & CMMN
notes.front: In a Decision Model and Notation (DMN) table with the Unique hit policy, what happens if two rows match the same input?
notes.back: The table is invalid for that input, because Unique allows at most one matching rule. Use First, Priority or Collect when overlaps are intended.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::06 DMN & CMMN
notes.front: A discount rule changes weekly. Why model it as a decision rather than as gateway conditions?
notes.back: Rules in a Decision Model and Notation (DMN) table can be changed and reviewed by business users without redrawing or redeploying the process, and the diagram stays readable.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::06 DMN & CMMN
notes.front: What is CMMN?
notes.back: Case Management Model and Notation (OMG): for unstructured, knowledge-driven work where the sequence can't be predetermined.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::06 DMN & CMMN
notes.front: Which OMG standard fits: (a) a predictable flow of steps, (b) eligibility rules, (c) an investigation whose steps depend on what's found?
notes.back: (a) BPMN; (b) DMN; (c) CMMN.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: What is business architecture (BCS)?
notes.back: A structured representation of an organisation's strategy, capabilities, value streams and structure, used to align business direction with change.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: Why use business architecture?
notes.back: It connects strategy to execution: assess change impact, remove duplicated effort, direct investment to the capabilities that matter most.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: What does business architecture give data, application and technology architecture, and what goes wrong without it?
notes.back: It supplies the business context and priorities they must support, keeping IT investment traceable to business need. Without it, technology is built to local demands and drifts from what the business needs.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: Typical impediments to adopting business architecture?
notes.back: No executive sponsor, unclear mandate, hard-to-show short-term value, and treating it as an IT-only concern.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: What is a T-shaped business architect?
notes.back: Broad knowledge across business, strategy and architecture (the bar) plus deep expertise in one area (the stem).

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: What does maturity of the business architecture practice range over?
notes.back: From ad hoc individual efforts with no method to an institutionalised, governed practice engaged in strategy and change decisions.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: Which context factors should drive the choice of a business/enterprise architecture framework?
notes.back: Fit with the organisation's size, sector and change context: a framework suited to one setting can be too heavy or too light in another.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: Beyond organisational fit, what practical criteria decide which architecture framework to adopt?
notes.back: How prescriptive it needs to be, which tools and skills already exist, and how well its artefacts map to real decision-making.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: BCS business architecture: view vs blueprint vs tool?
notes.back: View: a perspective (e.g. capability view). Blueprint: an artefact within a view (e.g. capability map). Tool: the technique/notation used to make it.
notes.analogy: View = the kitchen; blueprint = the recipe card; tool = the knife.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: What is 'business architecture as a service'?
notes.back: Running the practice as an internal service with its own value proposition to executives and change teams, not a one-off documentation exercise.
notes.source: BCS Business Architecture · BA as a Service

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: How does business architecture engage across the change lifecycle?
notes.back: Upfront: shapes strategy and investment. During delivery: informs design. Afterwards: checks change matches target capabilities.
notes.source: BCS Business Architecture · BA as a Service

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: Business architecture vs business analysis?
notes.back: Business architecture gives the strategic, cross-initiative context (target capabilities); business analysis works within one project and should align to it.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::07 Business Architecture Foundations
notes.front: How does business architecture help change and project management?
notes.back: Change management: clarifies what changes and why. Project management: target state and priorities to trace scope and business cases to.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: What does the motivation and organisational view analyse?
notes.back: The 'why' and 'who': purpose and values, mission/vision/goals, business model, structures, ecosystem and culture.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: Why do business motivation analysis?
notes.back: To make explicit why the organisation exists and what it aims for (mission, vision, goals, objectives, strategies), so later decisions can be justified against it.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: What does an ecosystem analysis examine?
notes.back: External parties (partners, suppliers, regulators, customers, competitors) and how value and influence flow between them.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: Business capability vs process?
notes.back: Capability: what the organisation can do — stable, independent of how or who. Process: how it's done — a sequence of steps that changes far more often.
notes.analogy: 'Can cook' is a capability; today's recipe is a process.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: A bank automates manual loan approval. Which changes, the capability or the process, and why?
notes.back: The process changes (new steps, new technology). The capability "approve loans" stays the same: it describes what the bank can do, not how.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: What makes up a business capability description?
notes.back: The people, process, information and technology needed to perform it (sometimes governance and culture too).

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: What is a capability heat map for?
notes.back: Colour-coding a capability map by a metric (importance, maturity, cost, risk) to show where investment is most needed.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: On a capability heat map showing importance and maturity, which capabilities merit investment first?
notes.back: Those that are high importance and low maturity: the biggest gap between what the strategy needs and what the organisation can do.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: In the process/service view, what is a service's value proposition?
notes.back: An explicit statement of the benefit the service delivers to its consumer — a check that it's designed around consumer need.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: Value stream vs business process?
notes.back: A value stream maps end-to-end value-adding stages toward a stakeholder outcome; it's outcome-centric and stable across redesigns. A process details how.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: How do capabilities relate to the stages of a value stream?
notes.back: Each value stream stage is enabled by one or more capabilities, so mapping capabilities to stages shows which capabilities a given outcome depends on.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: Value network vs value stream?
notes.back: A value network maps the web of value exchanges (revenue, information, goodwill) among many roles, not one linear sequence to one outcome.
notes.analogy: A value stream is a relay race; a value network is a marketplace.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: Information view: data vs information vs metadata?
notes.back: Data: raw facts. Information: data with context and meaning. Metadata: data about data (structure, source, owner, meaning).

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: What is business information modelling?
notes.back: A conceptual model of key business entities (Customer, Order) and relationships, independent of system design; linked to capabilities and processes.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: Competency vs capability in business architecture?
notes.back: Competency: an attribute of people (what a person/role can do). Capability: an attribute of the organisation, partly realised through competencies.
notes.extra: The people view examines skills, knowledge and behaviours.

notes.deck: BPMN & Business Architecture::08 Business Architecture Views
notes.front: What is organisational competency analysis used for?
notes.back: Finding gaps between current and required competencies, to inform workforce planning, training, hiring and org design.
